utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here, and I see a full house amongst the Defence teams. The Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic is soon going to finish his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, if you know, the whereabouts of my client, Ljubisa Beara, from July 17th through July 31st, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless otherwise noted in my narrative report, I don't recall that there is a specific intercept that reflects him, from the 17th through about the 22nd, 23rd. I think towards the end of July, there are specific intercepts which reflect his presence in association with Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. And we are talking about the period in association with Zepa, and an intercept that we reviewed or that you reviewed with Mr. McCloskey is dated the 1st of August, 1995, and that's why my question to you is specifically: From the 17th of July until the 31st of July, 1995, what did your analysis find as to the whereabouts of Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe we have any intercepts or any other information pertaining to his whereabouts during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you were going to be fair and objective in your report, isn't it something that you think you should put in your report, to say, "With respect to Mr. Beara, we do not know the whereabouts of where he was from the period of the 17th of July through the 31st of July, 1995"? Wouldn't that be fair to the man?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which report?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In any of the five that you wrote.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, with respect to the Srebrenica military narrative and the revised version, given that the focus is on Srebrenica and the Srebrenica crime bases, where he is included, his whereabouts after 18 July, with respect to the major crime scenes, his disappearance or his -- or a lack of awareness where he is wasn't relevant for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Help me with this, sir. Do you agree with me that you cannot and, in fact, were unable to document any significant crimes with respect to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding with respect to the crimes that occurred with Zepa is that they are charged with respect to forcible transfer and a few other legal things that I'm not sure of. We do not have, obviously, a collateral situation like one sees in Srebrenica, where you have the actual execution in large quantities of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll come back. Specifically, on the 17th of November, 2003, you stated that under oath, sir, on page 4675, lines 4 through 5, and I'll read it just so we have it clear: "Given that we don't have any significant crimes with respect to Zepa, to my knowledge," and then you proceed to discuss it. Are you telling us that forcible transfer, in your opinion, is not a significant crime, or, sir, is it in fact true that you believe, as you've testified under oath, that there weren't any significant crimes with respect to Zepa that you, as an analyst, found?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an analyst, I believe what I said, which is I don't believe that there are any significant crimes. As for whether or not forcible transfer is a significant crime within the context of the law is a question that, you know, I don't have the expertise to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when, if you can give us or help us with this timeline, when does that process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because this needs clarification, once you've raised it. What, in your mind, not having a legal background, do you understand by "significant crimes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Significant crimes with respect to the process of gathering people, moving them, and then the conduct of mass executions. I understand obviously there are legal discriminating factors between genocide or extermination or murder, but those are not within my field of expertise to make opinions on. The reality is it was a mass execution, how it's legally categorized. That's the view that I look at these issues when I say a major crime, "a mass execution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that's clear Mr. President, but if I can just follow it up on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very briefly. I just wanted to do establish when he uses the term "significant crimes," it's what he understands --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to focus a little bit on this Krstic tape that we saw during our trial, which I think has been identified as the "kill them all" tape. Do you remember that? It's an audiotape, actually; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think that under oath you stated previously that you were not to -- you were not prepared to conclude, based on that comment in isolation, that the intent behind the conversation was criminal in nature, and you held open the possibility that it may very well have nothing to do with the commission of any crimes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the logic that you used, the military analysis; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given when the audiotape was -- well, given when the actual intercept was taken and given my understanding of the military situation on the ground at the time, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And these things, when taken in isolation, can certainly have more than two meanings; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, which is exactly why I do as much of my analysis as I can in context, and not in isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the fair and objective and honest way to analyse; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proper way to analyse these things is in context, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Zepa, can you give us the timeline as to the date when the people were being either evacuated or transported from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the civilians were being transported from the Zepa enclave starting 26 July, if memory serves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We won't debate the dates with you, but we have other dates. When did it end, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, within two days, three days, the movement was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So would that be the 28th, 29th, according to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I believe I have the dates in my report, but I'm going off of memory here, so I think that the movement was only a day or two at max. It was not a very large movement process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take it at the outside to include it to be two days from the 26th to the 28th. Can you share with us what your analysis found as to where Ljubisa Beara was on July 26th, 27th, or 28th, when we discussed this transportation or evacuation of the civilians? Do you have any information whatsoever to identify his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, am I not correct, sir, that there is no evidence whatsoever with respect to Ljubisa Beara involved in the Zepa operation but for the intercepts that we see purportedly on the 1st and 2nd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, that's correct. I'm not aware of any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this also, sir. Is it correct that based on your analysis, there was no evidence that you saw or digested that Ljubisa Beara planned any part of this transportation or evacuation of the population from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that I can't comment on where he was and what he was doing, I mean, that is a logical inference to draw, that I can't and that I have no evidence that he was part of that. Whether it was true or not, I have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the same would go true, sir, for any purported organisation, assistance, supervision, facilitation; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same answer: I have no information, so, therefore, you know, on a lack of information, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look, if you don't mind, sir, at 65 ter 1378A, and that is the intercept of the 1st of August, 1995. And while that's coming up, I would just like to ask you a couple of preliminary questions, if you don't mind. You talk a lot about legitimate military activities in your report and, in part, in your testimony. You also talk about a legitimate military combat engagement. For our purposes, can you describe for me, what is a legitimate military combat engagement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A legitimate military combat engagement, it would be an engagement that falls within the confines of internationally-established Law of War. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where did you study this Law of War, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To finish the answer, obviously military officers aren't experts on that, and that is why, within the context of the VRS, those laws of war were codified within the service regulations on the Law on the Armed Forces with respect to that. So when I talk about the phrase "legitimate military combat," it is within the context of those SFRY regulations that the VRS adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, I think it is, when you say or use the contraction "aren't," you mean "are not experts"; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume, yes, sir, the military officers in question are not experts on international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking about you, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert on international law, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you're not an expert in criminal law, as we've established; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to law school. You can draw your own conclusion on that one, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have. Sir, with respect to that, we've used the word, and obviously somewhat incorrectly. For a legitimate military combat engagement, we've used the word "ambush" from time to time. Do you know what I'm referring to when I use the word "ambush"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In a military sense, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that what a military combat engagement is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one form of a tactical-level military operation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at this intercept, if you don't mind, of the 1st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's at 1002, if I have my notes correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, here it references -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Actually, it's on the second page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the last paragraph in the second page, which would indicate or start with the letter "B." Do you see that, where it says, "Know what, man ..."?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this intercept, we know there are basically two ways to identify a speaker, and one would be compromise, as you discussed, and the other one is voice recognition; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was another method that the intercept operators used.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: What, other than those two methods, are there, other than voice recognition and compromise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, depending on the context of the conversation, and even with respect to the use of call signs and the discussion that they're talking about, it's possible to make a fair inference on who the correspondents are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From a military or purported military analytical perspective or from an intercept operator perspective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, sir. For example, when -- excuse me. As I've talked before, when we see "Zlatar 01" personally involved in conversations, it's a fair inference to make that the individual in the conversation is, in fact, the Drina Corps commander, based on that compromise of a code name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, when we're talking about individuals, we're not talking about where they may have called. But when you have to identify an individual as a participant in a purported intercepted conversation, the two ways in which to identify them would be voice recognition and compromise; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, when talking about the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already answered that and also told you other factors as well. So let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was just trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this last paragraph, sir, it states here that it's alleged to have been purportedly Mr. Beara stating, "When we get it, we'll call the MKCK ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is there anything wrong with calling the International Committee of the Red Cross with respect to potential prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the abstract, certainly there's nothing wrong with any discussion with the International Committee of the Red Cross on prisoners of war, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, what is the standard for how long of a period of time do you have to register POWs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure what --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what international standards require. For the most part, though, the rule is that they're to be registered as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's kind of vague, but do you know what the United States government position is on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had to deal with that particular situation for a number of years, so I can't say I know what the current US government position is, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me show you an exhibit that I found of a recent article. And you're familiar with the International Herald Tribune, are you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a reliability newspaper, as far as you can tell; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as newspapers are reliable, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the Defence Department person by the name of -- I'm sorry, senior Pentagon official called Sandra Hodgkinson?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I have this marked as an exhibit, Your Honour, and let me read this. It's from the 7th of January, 2008, The Herald Tribune, and the article is entitled "Troubles at another prison run by the US."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll give it to you, sir, if the Court wishes, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, for the record, I forgot to mention that Ms. Schildge from the US Embassy has been present from the beginning of the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're not going to make me read that off the screen, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's on the second portion of that article, sir. And when they discuss this, the senior Pentagon official for detention policy, Sandra Hodgkinson, she refused to comment on the complaint, citing the confidentiality of communications with the Red Cross. She said that the organisations had access to "all Department of Defence detainees in Afghanistan after they are formally registered," and that "the military makes every effort to register detainees as soon as practicable after capture, normally within two weeks." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then she goes on to say something else: "In some cases, due to a variety of logistical and operational circumstances, it may take longer." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agree, disagree with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the statement that it takes 14 days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can he agree or disagree with a statement of someone with whom he's no relationship? The statement exists there in the newspaper. Don't ask him whether he agrees or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me try it this way, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're employed currently with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I interrupted, Mr. McCloskey. I didn't know what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Relevance was my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I can see some relevance. That's why I haven't stopped Mr. Ostojic as yet. We'll see as he goes along.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you work currently for Homeland Security, do you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you've testified a little bit about your background in connection with Homeland Security, and you state that in capturing POWs, it should be as soon as possible. Isn't it correct that the definition that the Pentagon department gives is actually more accurate, given that you work for the same government as Ms. Hodgkinson does, that, in fact, POWs are to be registered within four weeks -- or within two weeks, and sometimes it takes longer? Isn't that fair?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to your next question, Mr. Ostojic. I mean, let us decide. This is so marginal. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the record, my co-counsel is saying I didn't identify the exhibit number and I thought I did, but we'll find it for the Court and we'll get back to you. We'll have to get back to the Court with the exact exhibit number. I think we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's 2D157, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in isolation and in context, when we look at this intercept of August 1st, 1995, 65 ter 1378, there is nothing that's improper as to the contents of it, isn't that correct, from a military analytical standpoint?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the passage that I read, you're correct, there doesn't appear to be anything improper about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, not just from the passage that we've read. I mean, you've analysed this intercept. You've included it in your report. You've discussed it in your direct examination. What about the intercept do you find, if anything, that would constitute anything improper, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I do is what I'm saying. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That one intercept I don't see in that part; and, again, I didn't read the entire intercept because we just went to page 2. But for the context of what we talked about, I see nothing improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought you read the intercept before, sir, but I'll give you the opportunity, if you'd like, to read the intercept in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- yeah, that would be fine, sir, and then I can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, is this the first time you've seen this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, but I hope you'll appreciate my position. There has been a whole lot of documents that have been going by, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I do, sir. Now, let me ask you this: When, if -- when, to the best of your recollection, given that you left the OTP in November of 2004, as you've told us yesterday --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2003, sir. If I said "2004," that's a misstatement on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you for that clarification. You know, I'd hate to waste the valuable time that was given to me by the Court. If you'd like to read it, I'll give you the opportunity, since you asked to read it. I don't want to be accused of being unfair to you. But I'd like to move on, so it's really your call, sir. If you need to read it --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, you can proceed on, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next intercept, 65 ter 1380, and this is an intercept also purportedly capturing Mr. Beara at 2245.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir, at the top?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Among others, of course. And then what I'd like to do is focus quickly on the second page of that intercept, where it states that purportedly Mr. Beara is discussing ICRC escorts and for them to be exchanged here. Do you remember that at all? It's about a third from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is there anything wrong with that, sir, with having an ICRC escort and having the POWs exchanged at some point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not talking about their POWs. What they're talking about is what the Serbian MUP is doing with the POWs in Serbia, that -- as far as I can tell from this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, keep reading, sir: "We had no plans to kill them ... but to exchange them." Is Mr. Beara with the MUP at this point, according to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The context of the conversation, as I understand it, is they're talking about the activities of what the Serbian MUP are doing. That's how I -- that's how I understand the context of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar, sir, with respect to the intercept operators, if any of them were trained in voice recognition?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I don't know that yes or no, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in your analysis and participation and reliance on those intercepts, did you ever ask that question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I did not ask that question of the intercept operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to learn -- would you be surprised if none of them had experience in voice recognition?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It wouldn't surprise me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if the intercept operators ever had a dossier or a file of various VRS officers or military personnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't know that, that the operators would have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly, that's something you would have asked; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, sir, normally speaking, that's not material that the actual operators would routinely get. Their job is to collect the information, not to make judgements with respect to analysis at a higher level based on other forms of information. They're collectors, not processors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that it would be somewhat strange, if not unbelievable, that intercept operators would have dossiers on VRS officers or military personnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. If they had full dossiers on these individuals, I would agree that it would be strange, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you've never seen such dossiers from these military operators. They've never given you a copy of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only product I'm aware of is the general working notes of various operators with respect to frequencies and other technical data, not broader notes as you discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in your several or few meetings, interviews, that you've had with these intercept operators, that issue never came up; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of dossier or voice recognition?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dossier.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it never came up in your investigative team with Madam Stefanie Frease or Mr. Ruez; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge with respect to dossiers. I know that there was an effort to go out and obtain and clarify the relevant technical data that was incumbent in the intercept notebooks, but not with respect to analytical dossiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to just spend a minute, if we can, on compromise and to make sure that I understand it correctly. And that's for identification, voice identification. When we talk about compromise, there are two ways in order that an identity of a participant in a conversation can be compromised; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we've discussed, it's either a voice compromise, the individual compromises his own identity, or he's compromised by --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: By the other --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- yeah, by the other party. And then leading on to that, he's compromised by the context of his own conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: Did you discuss with any of the analysts, when there was no voice compromise, how were they able to deduce whether or not the speaker that they were purportedly intercepting the conversation was, was person A, B, or C?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. If it was not clear within the context of the conversation, whether it was a compromise or not, I took that into account in my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you would give it less weight, if you will?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, there are other factors. For example, if the compromise was not done prior to the actual contacts, there's certainly a possibility that as a component of the conversation, they would have recognised the voices of the individuals and used that accordingly. They were the best people who were taking that information at the time to make those judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll get to voice recognition in a second. But if we just stay with compromise, it would be fair that, as I said, you would give it less weight and, therefore, it would be less reliable; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the reliability of the correspondence we're talking about, I would give it less weight with respect to identity, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now let's turn to voice recognition. How often do you think that a person, such as an intercept operator with the level of experience, education, and certification that these gentlemen had, who are the intercept operators, how many times would they need to hear the voice of an individual participant so that it could be qualified as voice recognition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the expertise to answer that question, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it requires an expert opinion, Your Honour. I mean, simply put, it's the same level of expertise that we use every day when we recognise people we hear over a telephone. It's not a technical question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move, Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, as an analyst, albeit a historical analyst, did you address or analyse the NIOD report with respect to the intercept operators?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't analyse the NIOD report. I'm not even sure how much of it had been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to, if we may, turn to Srebrenica for a few moments. Sir, when we talk about the evacuation and the movement of the population of Srebrenica, can you give me, based on your analysis, what was that timeline? When did it start and when did it end?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the -- excuse me. I believe the first buses departed the Potocari compound at approximately between 1200 and 1400 hours. The convoys were suspended at darkness on the 12th. I believe they resumed as early as between 800 and 1000 hours on the 13th, and I believe that all of the individuals were evacuated by darkness on the 13th of July. I'm not aware of any information that there were still remaining, on the evening of the 13th of July, civilians that were going to be subsequently evacuated on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's talk about the visibility of Mr. Beara with respect to this period. Do you know the whereabouts of Mr. Beara from the beginning of July, and you can pick any date, but we can go with July 1st, up to and through July 13th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There's no information that I'm aware of with respect to intercepts or sightings that place Mr. Beara on the ground, with the -- I think the only exception that places him on the ground prior to the 13th is the identification of him by one Dutch officer at Nova Kasaba. I'm just unclear whether that identification is on 12 July or on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let's talk about or continue to talk about the visibility of Mr. Beara. You have no documentation and you've reviewed no such reports or information that he was ever at Srebrenica during that period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any military documents or video footage that put him there. I don't recall if statements by either Mr. Nikolic or Mr. Deronjic or other individuals place him on the ground or place him at Srebrenica. The town of Srebrenica, I just don't recall, but I don't believe that there is either video footage or documents that put him in the town of Srebrenica, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the same would be true with respect to Potocari, would it not, that there are no military documents or video footage or information that you've seen or analysed to put Mr. Beara in Potocari on or about that time period; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment Mr. Butler. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to avoid interrupting my client, but just at page 20, lines 7 and 8, the witness, Mr. Butler, mentioned a name "Nikolic." I'd just like him to confirm that we're not talking about Drago Nikolic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can. We're talking about Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Getting back to your question, sir: I don't believe so, but it's been a few years since I've actually seen the video coverage of Potocari. So I can't say that as an absolute fact, but I don't recall that I've ever seen video footage of him at Potocari or any documents that reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what about the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac? It's true, isn't it, that there's no evidence whatsoever that would place Mr. Beara at the Hotel Fontana at Bratunac for those what we've described as three meetings on the 11th and 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are some records that place him at the Hotel Fontana, that he has a room there during that relevant period. However, I'm trying -- I don't believe that he is listed as one of the participants in any of the three meetings, no, sir. I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have to break this down a little bit. What room records are you referring to, sir, that you claim Mr. Beara had a room at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- like I said, there are records that, as part of the Bratunac Brigade collection, that shows that a number of VRS officers, where essentially the Bratunac Brigade was paying for their rooms at the Hotel Fontana during this period. I don't recall whether or not Colonel Beara was one of those listed officers. I mean, we have those records, but I just don't recall at the moment whether he was one of those individuals who had a room or not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll take a look at that, sir, and I think your recollection will be refreshed that he was not. But in any event, you say in line 19, that he's not listed as one of the participants in any of the meetings. Aside from the lists, sir, I mean, we have video footage of those meetings, in part, do we not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the OTP has that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So let's not limit it to just a list. But all the documents that you've reviewed, including the video footage, all that which you're trying to put in this historical context for us that you reflect in your report, it's rather clear, is it not, that Mr. Beara was not - and you've concluded this, sir - he was not a visible figure in Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I basically said, as part of my report, if I recall correctly that particular paragraph, that he wasn't one of the listed participants at the meetings. That would be based off of, you know, lists, the material, as well as the video coverage. Whether or not -- I mean, there is testimony and there is other information that he was a participant in and around Bratunac at that time, but, you know, that's witness testimony, that's not documents or video.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And so why do you keep referring to it, Mr. Butler? I mean, you yourself said that you don't rely on that, you're not asked to rely on or analyse that witness testimony, you haven't done it. You're simply going to take the documents; and as Mr. McCloskey or my learned friend said, connect the dots or link them up to this historical analysis that you've done, but you seem to insist to want to talk about these interviews. That's not part of what your job is here, is it, to talk about those interviews?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But when you ask me a broad question that encompasses that information and want me to agree or disagree with it, I have to take it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm accepting that you're going to talk about the documents, that you're going to talk about the intercepts, and that you're going to use this analysis that you've come up with to put it in context. In the context of Ljubisa Beara, he was nowhere to be found, from those documents that you've reviewed, the intercepts, and the material that you've examined, in either Srebrenica, Potocari, or Bratunac, including the Hotel Fontana; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. It appears that there may be an alibi defence coming. I have no information from counsel of any alibi defence; and before any further questioning is going on, I think he should be ordered to follow the Rules of this Tribunal and provide us with alibi information. I have asked it repeatedly and received nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is also limited to the documents that the witness examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not and I don't want to get into a debate in front of this witness with what my learned friend said, but he's wrong to suggest that I'm not following the law, and he's wrong to suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because if you're going to proceed, then we have to do it in the absence of the witness. The thing is this: I am drawing a distinction between what you said, generally, and in the broader sense of the word, and, in fact, the question itself, which was limited to the documents that the witness examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection overruled, Mr. McCloskey. We need to remember that in the indictment, you also have "joint criminal enterprise." So what Mr. Ostojic may have in mind may not be that relevant for the time being, but what's more important is that the question is limited to the documents that the witness has reviewed, that is, intercepts and others, all the material that he has examined, either surveillance of Potocari or Bratunac including the Hotel Fontana. He hasn't answered that question, and he is being asked now to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: THE WITNESS: Yes, sir, for the 12th of July, that is correct. On the 13th of July, we start seeing intercepts that refer to the individual, depending on where various phone conversations are attributed to, and I believe there is one that attributes him to "Badem," which is the code name for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade on that date. I mean, that is an intercept document that potentially places him in Bratunac on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is the Court happy with the answer, and if I may proceed, in terms of did he answer the Court's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest that you move ahead, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me stick, then, with this, so we understand it correctly. And we'll get to that intercept on the 13th that you want to. Am I correct, sir, that Beara is not a visible figure in Bratunac in that period of time? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the period of time for the 12th of July, that's correct, from the documents and the intercepts, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about for the period of time after the 12th of July, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, for the 13th of July, his presence in and around Bratunac, and when I talk about in and around Bratunac, I qualify that as Bratunac Brigade, Nova Kasaba, and up the road, that road area there, I believe the intercepts reflect his presence on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I want to cover two little points with respect to this, and just so we're clear. So, prior to - although, you said, on the 12th of July, you agree there's no documents to support that he was present in Srebrenica, Potocari, Bratunac and/or the Hotel Fontana - but prior to the 12th of July, do you know what his whereabouts are, from the 1st through the 12th, up to and including this intercept of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not aware, incorporated in my reports or the material that I have seen, that I have any information about his whereabouts during that period through the 13th, when he becomes visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand what you said under oath on the 21st of November, 2003, in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's on page 5073, lines 11 through 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You go on to say: "And, again, Beara, it may well be; do they know who he is?" Then you go on to say: "He is not a visible figure in Bratunac." Then you go on to describe Momir Nikolic, among others, as being that people should know who they are on sight. I want to focus on the words that you used: "He," meaning Beara, "is not a visible figure in Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For that to be fair, we need to see the questions before and answers, but taking anything out of trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you have them available, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I've given the page cite. I only have my copy that the witness is more than happy -- I'm more than happy to give him my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think, at least if we put that on the ELMO, we can proceed at a faster rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I do have markings, Mr. President, on that, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see what markings they are. Let's put it on the ELMO. All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand the context of this comment, and I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First, is it true that Mr. Beara was not visible, according to your own sworn testimony, a visible figure in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- context of the conversation was whether or not visibility, not in the form of "I see you," but visibility in the form of somebody who is a figure in and around Bratunac and would be recognised by these individuals, and that's why, you know, individuals of the Drina Corps who are more habitually there, you know, would be recognised, such as Momir Nikolic. And individuals such as Ljubisa Beara, who would not be expected to frequent Bratunac, would not be recognised as readily, and that was the context that I made that comment about visibility on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me with this, and I want to stick to the period of time when the evacuation of the population started. That's the time period I want to start. That means everything that's involved in that that you, as a purported military analyst, knows. Up until the 12th of July, 1995, not only is Mr. Beara not physically visible, there's no documents whatsoever to indicate that he participated at all in any of the events leading up to the July 12th, 1995 evacuation of the population; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of the 12 July, there are no documents that reflect that, that's an accurate statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when you say "documents," you include the intercepts as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me with this, because my learned friend seems to be shocked about what he calls an alibi, but do you know of a newspaper reporter called Sredoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Prosecutor had called this person as a witness in their case-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that that person, Mr. Simic, interviewed Mr. Beara regarding some of the events involved in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor, at any time during your tenure here or during your proofing sessions for your testimony, inform you that in that interview, Mr. Beara says that during this time period, up until the 12th of July -- up until the 13th of July, 1995, that he was not at or around Srebrenica, Potocari, or Bratunac, or in that area? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm no aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that interview, Mr. Beara said that he was actually at -- in Bihac at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, since I don't know of the interview, I don't know what Mr. Beara said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could help us with that, sir. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If Mr. Ostojic is standing by that interview and the answers, as his duty regarding alibi, I would appreciate that, but that has never happened before. And if that's what he is saying, I think the law requires him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I don't want to sound cold-blooded, but we don't have a notice of alibi, in terms of Rule 67. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you help us understand, from your analysis of the documents, what, if anything, was going on in Bihac in that time period prior to the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you specifically what was happening in Bihac during that period. That was outside of my -- my area of review, so I don't know. I know in broad terms, but I don't know specifically what you would be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me in broad terms, and maybe we could connect it, like we would the --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In broad terms, the VRS military leadership was concerned about the potential that 5th Corps, as well as the Croatian Army forces, were going to launch a large-scale attack in the western part of the country. In that context, you know, there was a significant military interest in that particular region, the western part of the country. As for the actual details of what they were doing in preparation or to attempt to spoil that or other things, I don't know the answer. That's not an issue that I've looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or analysed; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look at it. Obviously, I didn't analyse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was the officer by the name of Manojlo Milovanovic; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He's the deputy commander of the Main Staff or -- I'm sorry. He is the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he was in that position in July of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. General Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic was in that position in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this, if you don't mind, from looking at the documents and analysing this case and spending time with the investigative team: Do you have any idea where Manojlo Milovanovic was in the early parts of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding that he was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was ever in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't, not during July of 1995. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now 65 ter number 480, which is a Prosecution document, and it's the article. I just want to be fair and put it to you, sir, since you've analysed all what you call relevant documents in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So 65 ter 480.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection on whatever that last comment was, but he's not stated that he's analysed every relevant document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me, then, ask the question. I thought that's what we got.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What relevant documents, sir, did you not analyse for purposes of your historical analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've indicated now for probably the fifth time, it's not a historical analysis; it's a limited analysis with respect to the military intercepts and the military documents and their correlation with the crime bases. This would be an example of a document that probably would not have made the cut, whether it's accurate or not, as relevant, because it has no particular relevance to a crime scene. I mean, I've never seen this before, so, I mean, I'm kind of commenting in the abstract on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I can imagine. Do you think that's something that you should have been given, so that you could at least digest it and make the determination as to whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we're sticking with the time period up through and including the start of the process for evacuation, and I want to make sure. You've seen not one order, not one military document, not one directive, not one intercept, not one piece of evidence to indicate that Mr. Beara was in any way involved with any of the process with respect to the evacuation or the movement of the people from either Srebrenica or Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not delaying. I'm just going down through your checklist. You've asked a lot of questions here. Yes, sir, I believe that that's correct, as long as we're fair that whatever witnesses may or may not potentially say is not what I'm including in your context of one piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we know that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to be clear on that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You've said it several times and we accept that, and thank you for repeating it, but we know that. It's just from your analytical standpoint, from the documents that you've reviewed, and my question was limited, just so you can rest comfortably. Okay? So, I know it's limited to that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I believe that that's accurate. I'm not aware of any information that with respect to the movement of the people from Srebrenica or Potocari, in the context that we're talking about, the civilian movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to the column, if you don't mind. During your -- and, I'm sorry, I thought we had called it yesterday "historical analysis," and I didn't mean to offend you if think it's not --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You've called it that. I've been consistent --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- about what I've called it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, sir, you called it that under oath in the Blagojevic case, but we'll look at that record again. With respect to your analysis, did you analyse at any time how many military combat engagements were there with respect to the column of Bosnian Muslims that were leaving Srebrenica and Potocari from Susnjari and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I never engaged in a process to do a step-by-step accounting of each particular engagement of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go a little broader. Did you ever engage in a process to do something more general than this step-by-step accounting that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. In fact, based on the information that I had, I worked to be able to establish the track of the column from where it left, and particularly once it crossed over the road -- excuse me, the Konjevic Polje-Milici road and went through the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, so I could track the broad movement of the column in point of location on the ground and in point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Butler. I'm really actually referring to the combat engagements. Did you track where, specifically, these military combat engagements occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't track specifically, other than the general references to ambushes at Snagovo, at various terrain features that were listed in the brigade combat reports on the 12th, 13th, and 14th. I did not track specific -- or did not make an effort to track specific combat activity of the column, 12th and 13th, south of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you can't tell us, as you sit here, how many military combat engagements were undertaken during that period of time in July of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you've called and you've used the word "legitimate military combat engagement," and do you agree with me, sir, that these were, indeed, legitimate military combat engagements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a result of the mixed character of the column, with a mixture of military units and personnel and civilians, I believe I've been fairly consistent by saying that, you know, regardless of the civilian presence, that, you know, at face value, it would qualify as a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I asked you if you analysed when and where these legitimate, if we can call them now, with your opinion, legitimate military combat engagements occurred. Did anyone else, to your knowledge, any of your other assistants, or associates, or anyone on the investigative team, actually sit down and do a step-by-step process of where these legitimate military combat engagements occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not to my knowledge, or certainly not to the degree that you're talking about. The only ones that was done, to my knowledge, is the ones that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in order to give an objective, fair balance, or a conservative approach to any analysis, wouldn't that be something that should be included in a report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, given what the goals of my report were, if I were prepared to concede that the column was a legitimate military target, any casualties related to that particular operation would, by definition, be lawful. Given the context of what we were looking at with the crime base, it didn't matter what happened to the column, per se. It only mattered what happened to the individuals after they came into the custody of the VRS after being captured or surrendered. That is why that particular type of analysis that you have looked for was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so I'm clear, so when you say "legitimate" in your report, especially or specifically when you reference "legitimate military combat engagements," you're really saying "lawful military combat engagements," are you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say "legitimate military combat engagements" because the column represents a military target. I will concede that particularly in this institution, there will be and no doubt will continue to be a debate as to at what point and juncture so many civilians changed the character of not only a column but any other military objective. That's why I took myself out of that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't know that you have, but thank you for your analysis of that. But on page 35, line 1, you, in fact, state that -- you mean that "legitimate" means lawful, does it not, in your opinion? Don't worry what everyone else thinks about. You're the one who is under oath here as a witness in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's calling for a legal opinion which Mr. Butler has not made, and I don't think it's appropriate. These are not items that are part of the charges of the indictment, either. So where are we going?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir - and maybe I can direct a little more attention to where we might be going with it, since my learned friend doesn't know - did you analyse at any time, sir, whether there were minefields on that stretch from Susnjari through to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was, in fact, aware that there were minefields not only around the enclave but that there were minefields particularly between the confrontation lines between the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and the ABiH 2 Corps people close to Tuzla. We had heard that there were potentially uncharted minefields along some of the smuggling routes that some of the units, whether the Zvornik or the Milici or the Bratunac Brigades, might have placed along areas that they thought that the ABiH was smuggling in weapons, but I -- I'm not aware whether or not those have actually been located. So, I mean, while I've heard rumours of those types of minefields, I don't know them as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So how many minefields were there, Mr. Butler? Three?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a distinct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ten?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mining records exist. I just never -- I can't give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how many people -- or strike that. Who, on the investigative team that you were involved in, was in charge of determining how many minefields there were? Who was the person who would be in charge of that, in reviewing these landmine records that you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you ask Mr. McCloskey, and he will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you, as a military expert, in your report analyse how many people died as a result of coming into contact in landmine fields or landmines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't. I didn't analyse ABiH military casualties at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let me restrict it again and confine it, and thank you for that. It's quite clever. Confine it to the column that we're talking about, sir. With respect to the column that left from Susnjari to go towards Kladanj and Tuzla, do you know, sir, or did you ever analyse how many people died as a result of landmines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I thought I just answered that question. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you know of anyone on the investigative team -- sir, do you know of anyone on the investigative team who actually has conducted any sort of analysis whatsoever to determine how many people from the column that left from Susnjari to go towards Tuzla died as a result of landmines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not that was a function of one of the OTP forensics teams that were part of the investigation or not. I mean, I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. My next question with respect to this column, sir, is: Did you personally analyse how many people died as a result of these legitimate combat military engagements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've given the numbers of VRS casualties, but I told you I did not analyse ABiH casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't relevant to my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it relevant to determine how many people may have died during the period in Srebrenica in July of 1995, to distinguish whether some of them died from legitimate military combat engagements? Isn't that really what you're saying, that that's not relevant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would only be relevant if the forensics evidence of the mass graves were showing evidence that would reflect that the bodies in those graves reflected combat casualties. The forensics evidence, as I understand it coming out of those mass graves, reflects the opposite, that they're not combat casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's based on -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's based on your recollection of the summary of these forensic pathologists who have reviewed the material; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, that was a -- one of the very first -- when we talk about holding analytical options open, when I first started here, that was one of the obvious options that I felt that you do explore, whether or not the bodies that were in the mass graves were not victims of crimes or alleged crimes, but who are, in fact, casualties that would have occurred in combat. So that was an option that I held open, and the forensics teams were able to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did you have these discussions with the forensic teams, specifically with respect to the issue of whether any of the bodies that were found in the mass graves were or were not as a result of legitimate military combat engagements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have specific discussions with the forensics people. However, because I was incorporated into the investigations, as I was continuing to do my analysis, and particularly as they were also working concurrently on the forensics, you know, we were able to conclude, particularly with respect to Zvornik, that the individuals that were coming out of these particular mass graves and the associated secondaries, you know, were not meeting the characteristics of combat casualties, in fact they were meeting the characteristics of victims from crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll revisit some of that. Thank you. What I'm asking you now, sir, is: Do you know, based on the materials that you reviewed, what the number is of these -- strike that. From your review of the materials in the time that you spent with the Office of the Prosecution, do you know, sir, what the number of deaths were there as a result of the legitimate military combat engagements from the side of the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you, sir, that the Office of the Prosecution has taken witness statements from witnesses which indicate that in, for example, one particular combat engagement, over a thousand people died as a result of this legitimate military combat engagement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not surprise me that a witness would say that. I would think that from my knowledge of the situation, that that number would be high for any particular combat engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there are witnesses that say that there were, in fact, 1.000 to 2.000 people from the column that died as a result of these combat engagements? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a gross period from 12 to 18 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not aware of the engage -- I'm not aware of the specific number, but that particular number of 1.000 to 2.000 sounds reasonable, given the context of the combat that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you're saying that, including all of the combat engagements, correct, as opposed to one isolated combat engagement? Would that be fair, if I can understand what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I think the 1.000 to 2.000 number would be reasonable with respect to the combat casualties starting, you know, from 12 July through the life span of the column, which is effectively 18 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time, sir, consider this sworn testimony from these Bosnian Muslims who survived and were either captured or made it to Tuzla and their description of the number of combat casualties in any of your analyses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in speaking or in telling us that one of the options was to consult with these forensic pathologists, do you remember if you told them that, in fact, of the mass graves that they'll uncover, there may be bodies in those mass graves that would include people who were -- who suffered injuries or ultimate death as a result of these combat engagements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That the number -- sorry. Let me throw this in so I don't have to -- we're getting near the break: And that the number can be as high as 1.000 to 2.000?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I didn't give specific guidance to any forensics people. The forensics part of the investigation began well before my tenure at this institution; and, particularly, when I started my own military analysis, I mean, it was clear to the investigative team that I was interested in, you know, having, you know, confirmation, one way or another, that, you know, relevant gravesites that we were looking at were, in fact, the results of criminal activity and not the results of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But where are those people and the bodies, the corpses of those people who unfortunately died as a result of the legitimate military combat engagement with the VRS during their trek from Susnjari through to Tuzla? Even if the number, as you suggest, is as low as 1.000 or as high as possibly 2.000, where are those bodies located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, particularly in the early postwar years, was because of the high threat of uncharted minefields and uncharted or unexploded ordinance, that there was no effort made for many years to go in and attempt to recover those surface remains. I think that I recall, somewhere around 2001 and 2002, the Bosnian government felt it was safe enough to start doing that, but I'm not aware of how many remains that they've ever collected or things of that nature. But, I mean, I know that particularly in the early post-war years, there was a deliberate decision not to try and police up those remains because of the ordinance and mine threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just before the break, I just have a couple of other questions unrelated to this, specifically, but related more to your broad analysis, or generally your analysis, if I can say that. Now, you've in the past, in testifying both in the Krstic and in the Appeals -- with the Appeals Court in Blagojevic, and you've conceded that you, as an analyst, and I think even during your direct, you've conceded, as an analyst, that you have made some misinterpretation of several things; like an intercept, for example. You know what I'm referring to; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, analysts such as yourself - and we've seen, although we won't use the example of analyst intelligence, analysts who show aerial photographs to the United Nations for weapons of mass destruction that ultimately are not proven. We're not going to ask you that - but you concede, sir, that given, given your limited analysis, as you suggest, and looking at only some of the documents, that there is indeed and could be error in some of your findings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly will concede up front that there is a possibility of error in my findings, absolutely. And for the record, the Secretary of State is not an analyst. He was the one who showed the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with who Colin Powell is, but, sir, do you think that he actually showed the photographs without consulting with any intelligence analyst before showing them to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, who else assisted you in the preparation of your reports, both on the brigade, the corps, the Main Staff, your narrative, and then the revised narrative, historical analysis, that you provided to us? Who, if anyone, assisted you in that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I indicated yesterday my partner with the analysis was Ms. Amanda Brettell. She is also a MAT analyst. She has a police background and a research background, not necessarily a military one. My research assistant was a Ms. Sally Lattin, and we had a number of translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All he could have just said was the same people identified yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who, in particular, assisted you with the analysis on the Main Staff narrative that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Brettell was responsible in part with I think some of the young interns for helping to assemble material and send it back to me. But in that particular context, I drafted that report myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're near the break time. I'm moving into another subject when we come back, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you have, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe an hour and a half, Mr. President, although it's difficult to gauge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're almost done, Mr. Butler. A few more areas that I'd like to cover with you. Sir, I'd like if we can turn now to the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in particular, with the assistance of the Court, if we could have document 65 ter 2518 on the screen, and it was also identified under the number 2754 as well. So I'm not sure what number they may be using, and it bears the ERN number 0427983. Just so that we're accurate. Okay. Apparently, we don't have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But I can still ask the preliminary question, if you don't mind, Mr. Butler, while they're finding that. This is a report, do you recall, that you discussed with my learned friend during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that in this report, there was, at least during your proofing session, there was some handwritten material that was located on the top right-hand corner? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handwritten material, insomuch as -- I mean, there's a notation that says, "Handwritten: Files." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you show him straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have one copy here. Maybe we could place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
