utterances.text: Thank you for being practical, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I see the handwritten in -- on that version, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. You discussed that handwriting, did you not, during your proofing sessions with Mr. McCloskey, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. If -- it might help if I -- I don't recall whether I had it translated or not, so, I mean, I don't recall at this juncture whether I did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, just for my learned friend, if he looks at his proofing session notes of Mr. Butler, on page 14, paragraph 7, he discusses that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You discussed it and state that. Quote, in the third paragraph again on page 14, under paragraph 7, discussing this document, it states: "In relation to the handwritten note at the top of the document, Butler stated that the reference," and then it goes on to discuss what the references are. Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would probably remember it in context to what the reference was, if you could refresh my memory as to what it actually says.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it says there: "50 MUP men." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get a full reading? There's been quite a few of these notes on various documents, and I don't remember it either. If we could read the whole thing, maybe that will help refresh the recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic. How much can you help us there?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not much, but I can read what's said in the proofing note; and as I think as I cited, it's on page 14 of the proofing note. It says as follows, Mr. Butler, to put it in context, may you can help us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we don't have that, as you know. But go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the third paragraph, it says: "In relation to the handwritten note at the top of the document, Butler stated that the reference to '50 MUP men' may be connected with the arrival of a company of military police from the East Bosnia core in the Zvornik area on the 15th July 1995; to a Sekovici unit from Bratunac who also arrived in the Zvornik area on the 15th July 1995, or a group of municipal police from Doboj, whose commander was captured by the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Now I remember that, that handwritten notation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, because we're trying with your evidence, I think, to keep things in context, help us contextually, if you will, when was this commander captured by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the MUP commander in question was captured either late night 14th or the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, this letter or this exhibit that we're looking at also discusses reinforcements, does it not? I think that was part of your testimony on direct; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is: You said and set out that there's approximately, if not only three, but at least three variations as to who the reference may be to these 50 men. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's a reasonable approach, and I'm sure you'll agree, is it not, to an analyst, to list out all the different options that he thinks they may be referencing to if you're going to interpret or analyse such an entry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now it talks also in that report, reinforcements related to this commander who was captured, but also reinforcements for other reasons; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it was somewhat awkward. When you list out the three options, you identify three particular units; and for the third unit, according to the proofing note we got from Mr. McCloskey, you say that it could be related to a group of municipal police from Doboj whose commander was captured by the Muslims. What my question is, with respect to the other two options: Do they have anything to do with this commander that was captured from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The military police from Bijeljina were VRS, so I don't believe they're in context to that particular one. There were -- there was another municipal police unit that came in obviously from the Sekovici one. I don't believe that the military commander was from that one, either. So, I mean, I only -- I only note that because it's my understanding or at least my recollection that it was the commander of that particular unit who was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the time, if you could look at the time stamp ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And maybe help us by just moving the paper a little higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: ... when that document was either created or sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the -- what appears to be the receipt stamp on it is "15 July," then I see a zero, and it may be another zero or not, but I can't tell. There's one notation that says "15 July," and there's a second one under the -- hold on one second. I can't make out the second one, because it says "16", and I'm not sure, but that looks like either a "08" or "09" or something. So I don't know that I can make sense out of that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You don't know that it says 8:00 or at any other given time; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I can't make that out at what time it says. The reproduction is just too blurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the time stamp there, does that indicate when it was initially sent, or can you help us understand the time stamp just a little bit better?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My indication of the document that we're talking about on the ELMO, this particular stamp at the bottom is a time stamp that indicates when it was received, not a "sent" stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there any indication as to when this document was prepared and sent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a 15 July 1995 date on it, and it may be possible, in the English language version, that from the context of the document, you might be able to further divine at least which times they were talking about something happening prior to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this document, they're talking about reinforcements to be used for three to four days, are they not? Do you see that plainly on the second paragraph of the document? Even though it's B/C/S, I think you can make out "3-4 dana," which is three to four days?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's turn, if we can, to the 15th of July, 1995, and the purported intercept with Mr. Beara, which has a 65 ter number 1178.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, as you may know, as they're placing this document up, if I can just ask you, if you recall, there are actually more than one purported transcriptions, if you will, of this conversation of the 15th of July, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe, on this particular one, there's somewhere between -- on this one with General Zivanovic, there's two. I think there's -- there may even be a partial floating around as well. I don't know that we've incorporated that, but I know there are multiple versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In looking at this document, can you tell me if the intercept operator used either voice recognition or compromise to identify the participants in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this, it appears that General Zivanovic has been voice compromised. Can you scroll down, please, to the bottom in English? Thank you. It does not appear that Lieutenant-Colonel Beara has been voice compromised.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It not only not appears, it's rather clear, is it not, that there was no voice compromise relating to the identity of the person who this purported operator believes is, as he puts, Colonel Ljubo Beara; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn, sir, to the next intercept of the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for the record, I'm being told, just so that we have a clean copy or a correct version of the record, that what we were looking at was 65 ter 1378 and not 1178. But if there is a confusion on that, I was just given this sheet. I think it's 1178. But with all due respect, I just want to put that on the record, so that we don't have any confusion. But I think we've identified it sufficiently enough as the intercept at 0954 hours on the 15th of July. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Turning to the next intercept that we have of the 15th July 1995, that would be 65 ter 1179. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, how many different intercept operators purportedly captured this conversation between allegedly a Colonel Ljubo and Krle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you intercept operators. My recollection is that there are two versions of this, as well as a partial version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that would make it three, would it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I mean, I don't know -- I mean, I can't put it to a direct operator, but, I mean, I'm telling you how many versions that I know are in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll have you look at this quickly and then we'll look at the other two, just so you have the complete grouping of these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the next exhibit, if we can just have, I have it marked as 1179H, as in "Henry."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This would be another version of this intercept purportedly captured on the 15th of July, 1995, just a slightly different time period. The first one, and you can take my word for it, I believe, was at 0955. And the second one is at 0957. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then the third one, just so you can take a look at it, is under 65 ter number 1179C, as in "cat." This, sir, has a time of 1000 hours. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Those are the three versions, if we could call them, or the three intercepts that were purportedly captured on the 15th of July, 1995, at or approximately 10.00, between allegedly Mr. Beara and Mr. Krstic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you link, given the time scope of this document, this intercept with any potential reinforcements that may be asked for by anyone from the Main Staff, such as the documents that we just saw, 65 ter 2518, also using the number 2754? Did you make any link or connect the dots with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you link this intercept of the 15th of July, 1995, with the document that's on the ELMO, with the handwritten material that we've just discussed moments ago? Did you connect the dots there at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in this intercept, and I'm generalising, you claim that Mr. Beara is asking for 30 or so men; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what the intercept says, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in the document that's on the ELMO, there's a reference to 50 or so men, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In this intercept of the 15th of July, 1995, at approximately 10.00, there's a reference to three days, is there not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in the document that we have in front of you on the ELMO, which we thought, although we'll have to amend it, which is 65 ter 2518, there's a reference to three to four days, is there not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How do you, sir, as a reasonably prudent person, how do you not include that the men that were being requested were not requested for the same reason as that which you list with respect to this exhibit, 65 ter 2518, and the notation that we see on the top right-hand corner on the ELMO of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, first of all, in the context of the intercepts, the men that he's been asking for particular men for two or three days. In the context of the reinforcements from the Krajina Corps, there's no information that anyone has been asking for them for two or three days. So I think it's an "apples and oranges" type of argument. Boban Indjic and individuals from Visegrad are not to be confused with people coming in from the 1st Krajina Corps. The other issue is that, while this particular 15 July Main Staff order wasn't available for me when I was doing my analysis with the reports, I did have other information with respect to documents from the Zvornik Brigade and Bratunac Brigade, as well as from the RS police, which laid out those particular units that the reinforcements were coming from. So because I already had that, I was able to exclude that particular avenue of analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's -- thank you for that. Let's look at the comment that you attribute or that they attribute to Mr. Beara, where he says, "I've been waiting three days." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is it reasonable to, when you analyse this, to say that Beara has not done anything for those three days prior and he's simply waiting for three days, from the 12th, 13th, and 14th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I take, within the context of that intercept, that the order was given three days prior for these individuals to arrive and that he is, in fact, still waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you find an order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There is no written order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So are you making an assumption here, sir, with respect to this order that we have no documentation of, that you claim in your analysis is as to what occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not making an assumption at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Butler, that it's pure speculation on your part, since you have no corroborating evidence whatsoever, that there was even such an order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, because, in fact, there is corroborating information with respect to another intercept, related to the fact that a vehicle supposedly carrying these individuals from Visegrad had broken down. So in that respect, there is. But, you know, I agree with you also that there is no written order deploying these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've connected that intercept or that purported intercept of a few days earlier with this intercept, but you refuse and don't want to connect this intercept, which is temporally, date and time-wise, on all four squares with the material that you have on the ELMO requesting reinforcements, the number of reinforcements, and the number of days. How do you make that illogical conclusion, with all due respect, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because logically for me the infantry company from the 1st Krajina Corps has absolutely no relationship to a group of men coming from the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, which is a Drina Corps asset. It's apples and oranges. They're discussing two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you list, on the data that we have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please make breaks between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might help if I could see the transcripts on my screen. That way, I would know. I didn't know it was something I could do. I'm sorry. Thank you very much. Hopefully, that will help pause us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you, with respect to the exhibit that's on the ELMO, which has a 65 ter number 2518, and just so the record is clear, it has the handwritten information on the top right-hand corner that we've discussed, why didn't you, during your direct examination, while discussing reinforcements, tell us that you saw a different exhibit with handwriting information on it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe, as is evidenced when you started your line of questioning on this, I didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, certainly, you didn't incorporate that in any of your analyses because you didn't have a chance to review it but for during the proofing sessions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir. I want to ask you a couple more questions in connection with that intercept. Can we see where purportedly Mr. Beara is during this conversation? You're welcome to use any of the three intercepts that we have.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's okay. Just waiting for it. Could you scroll down to the bottom, please. Okay. The next page, English, please, or is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: While you're looking at that, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could just ask the Court to ask the usher to return the document that's on the ELMO. We're done with that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I've read it. I do not believe, in any of this version of the intercept, there is a compromise or any indication that you could attribute a physical location of Colonel Beara at the time. I believe that I make that observation of where he's located from the prior intercept, which gives a "139" phone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just so I understand, sir, you can have compromise both with respect to the identity of the participants and the location; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, any amount of -- you can have any number of compromises within context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in your analysis - and I'm trying to just go a little slower as a courtesy - in your analysis and in keeping this in context, are you familiar with how the switchboard operator was able to connect incoming calls from two parties that may be calling that specific operator?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't have a detailed knowledge of how the switchboard worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who, in the investigative team, would have that purported detailed knowledge as to how the switchboard worked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we just have a little more definition. Which switchboard?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Take any switchboard. Well, let me give you the hypothetical, that you're the switchboard, Mr. Butler, that I call you and that my learned friend Mr. McCloskey calls you to your right. Do you know that they had a capacity to actually put Mr. McCloskey's call to my call, even though we were not either at Mr. McCloskey's place or your place, where the switchboard operator was? Did you know they had that capacity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I don't know the capacities of the local switchboards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who would in the investigative team that you worked for involving the Srebrenica issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So, as an analyst, do you think that that is something that may be lacking in order to determine whether or not someone is at a given place, if you don't have a full and complete understanding of how the switchboard worked?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it is a piece of information that I would have liked to have had at the time, but I didn't think that in the context of the other information that I had, that it was a critical piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if you're saying that someone is at a certain area, whether it's an IKM, for example, and if you make the assumption that as a result of this call, person X is at the IKM in Zvornik, and if you don't know how that switchboard worked, your analysis could be actually deficient and in fact wrong, because that person may have just called in that IKM and was connected with another individual; wouldn't that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe your hypothetical is wrong, because I've never said the IKM. My analysis of where the correspondents are talking in this intercept is that General Krstic is at the Drina Corps IKM that was established for Zepa, and that based on the phone number attributed to where Colonel Beara can be reached in the prior intercept, that he is located at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, not the IKM, because the number is attributed to the phone number of Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's that 139 phone number; correct? "Extension," I should say.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in your analysis, did you find whether or not that 139 extension is attributed to anyone else other than Drago Nikolic, allegedly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My -- my analysis reflects that the 139 number was the number for the security office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you'll be asked some questions about that, so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the intercept that I think the Prosecutor has coined from time to time as the triage intercept, which is dated the 16th of July, 1995, and it has a 65 ter number 1187, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if you could just be kind enough to take a look at that purported intercept of the 16th of July, so that I can ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, from my reading of this, "triage" is used on four separate occasions, the specific word, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'll take your word on that one. I guess I don't have to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but you're welcome to do so. And how many times does purportedly Mr. Beara use that word?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that that particular phrase is associated with the correspondent Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where is the individual X?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the X is identified at Cerovic, at that point time, Colonel Cerovic is the duty officer of the Drina Corps. He would be in Vlasenica, at the Drina Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, will you agree with me that the word "triage," as mentioned in this purported intercept, can have multiple meanings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can have multiple meanings, yes, sir. Within the context of this intercept, though, I believe it has only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember, sir, in your testimony under oath in the Krstic case on the 19th of July, 2000, you also said that there's a military meaning of the term which pertains to the separation of wounded on medical grounds? In fairness to you, and I'm sorry, I should give the page number. It's on page 5357, lines 11 through 12. You begin by saying, "In fairness, sir, the military lexicon defines the term in a medical sense." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. I recall that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you go on, if I can, from lines 11 through 24, again on page 5357, during your testimony in the Krstic case on the 19th of July, 2000. "I would hesitate to get very far down the road, speculating what the phrase 'triage' might mean. In various other forms of potentially criminal or non-criminal applications, it is the word that they used. And as I generally note, I try not to put additional or more meaning into their words than is self-evident." Do you remember that sworn testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then the Honourable Judge Riad asked you, because he wasn't sure was meant by "self-evident": "What do you mean by self-evident?" Then you proceed to answer the question as follows: "Sir, they use the phrase 'triage.' One possible explanation, is as Mr. Petrusic forwards, there could be multiple possible explanations. All I'm saying, as part of my analysis, is here's the word that was used as translated, and I would prefer not to try to speculate as to what they really mean behind that individual word, sir." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, wouldn't you agree with me, in keeping in mind one of your fundamental components of your analysis, that you're trying to be as conservative as possible, that you cannot infer from the text of the intercept alone that there was any dark connotation, as I think you refer to during the Vasic identification document and the word "killing," attached to the use of the word "triage"? Wouldn't you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the abstract of this intercept, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time on the 15th of July, 1995, and I know we -- or 16th, I'm sorry, 16th of July, 1995, we discussed the column and some of the -- that's from these legitimate military combat engagements. Are you familiar, sir, that there was statements that the Prosecutor received from Bosnian Muslims, who were in the column, who identified during this time period that there were many hundreds wounded as a result of these legitimate military combat engagements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And particularly seven years ago, during the Krstic trial, I held that possibility open because the investigation had not been able to either confirm or deny or identify the numbers of potentially wounded combatants that might be in the custody of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. Seven years down the road now, the investigation has been able to run that particular issue to ground; and because of that and because now I have a better understanding of the context, I'm more willing to exactly give you what I believe the phrase "triage" means in the context of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want you to speculate, sir, as you've said that that's what it would mean.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know, during your proofing session with Mr. McCloskey, whether you discussed if other former VRS officers ever used the word "triage"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't recall that came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your review of the documents and the material in total that you reviewed, did you ever find that some or any officers would use the word "triage"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, as a component of the investigation, that question was asked to a number of individuals in this particular context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe General Zivanovic was asked that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if Major Golic was asked that question as of conduct of his interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about Mr. Cerovic, was he asked?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the investigation had ever interviewed Colonel Cerovic. I understand he either was interviewed and at some point in time stopped, or didn't consent to be interviewed. I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, wait. He's a participant of this supposed July 16, 1995 intercept, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Don't you think it might be reasonably prudent that the Office of the Prosecution would have interviewed another participant in this purported conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Office of the Prosecutor had meaningful subpoena power to be able to do that, I'd say yes; but we don't and we do not have the ability to go to Serbia and demand people show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about this, sir, the use of the word "triage"? If we're discussing the column of the 28th Division passing through, do you remember if an officer ever said that, "We do not try to carry out a triage to see who was a civilian and who wasn't"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- do I remember if an officer ever -- could you provide more information on who the officer might be? That's pretty abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. Let's just take it one step at a time. In that sentence, if it's true, "triage" in that sense is being used to separate civilians from military combatants or soldiers, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that, you know, in that, it could be used in that context. That would be a definition that would make sense, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I'm just looking for a little guidance, but may we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, given what we've seen now in private session and - I know we're in open. Yes, thank you. Just so it makes sense later - and the fact that you did not have any material from the person who used the word "triage," whether it's X or this C which is attributed to Cerovic on the 16th of July, 1995, we can see, if we actually study hard, that there can be multiple reasons or multiple -- strike that, multiple definitions of this military lexicon, as you put it under oath in the Krstic trial, of the word "triage"; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the word itself has multiple meanings, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to put into focus, if we can, if we take words in isolation, we saw that the Dragomir Vasic letter -- or, I mean, I'm sorry, the document, which is dated, and I have it here --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 886.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You testified - if I may proceed while it's being brought up to the screen - on the 17th of July -- I'm sorry, 17th of January, 2008, the reference to that word "killing," and you said, and you gave your identification about it, that, "It has no dark meaning." Do you remember that, pages 19870, lines 10 through 14?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, while the word itself has multiple meanings, it's my interpretation of what the word implies within the context that it's being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, also, I think, in another example of the utilisation perhaps of the word "kill" or "killing" is the Krstic tape, and I think you also at that point came to the same conclusion, that despite that the word "kill" was used, that it didn't have a dark connotation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, or it had multiple connotations. At that -- and my analysis at that time, I didn't attribute it a darker or murderous intent, which may be a more accurate way to say it, to that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to discuss, if you will, a little bit a different area, and that is internal affairs. Do you generally know what internal affairs is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume we're referring in a law enforcement perspective, internal affairs or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take it first from a law enforcement perspective, and then we'll move to a military perspective.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, law enforcement perspective, my understanding of "internal affairs" is a group of individuals who investigate the activities of law enforcement officials to ensure that they're functioning in compliance with law and not themselves using their official functions to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Investigating their own people within their unit or organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what about in a military setting, how would you describe an internal affairs officer or an internal affairs person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you how it is in a broader military setting. I am sure that the US military's, you know, criminal investigation division may have those; although, I don't know that. So, I mean, I couldn't tell you how that function works within a military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the VRS, in that context, I think I can give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the VRS, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. In that context, it would be those investigative activities to ensure that military officials are, again, operating in compliance with law and regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who would they be? Who would really be identified in this term of art "internal affairs" in the VRS military, based on your analysis of the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There's no foundation that this term "internal affairs" has been used in any military context at all, and so the form of the question is incorrect. This is a -- this is a term from American television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic has very little opportunity to watch here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Although, I am rather offended by the comment, I won't go into an argument about it now, but I think the witness answered the question both in terms of law enforcement and military, and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's understandable why he has answered the question, too. So let's hear what Mr. Bourgon has to say, coming to the rescue. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has referred to internal affair organs on a number of occasions in his reports. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that he has. I know that he has, but is it necessary to dwell on this matter any longer, Mr. Ostojic, or shall we move ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, it is necessary, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very briefly, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Which organ of the VRS would have the function and the duties and responsibilities to that which is equivalent to what you, sir, have identified, whether it's from your personal experience in law enforcement or your experience in the military, taking aside anything you may have gleaned from television, who would be similar to that as an internal affairs person? What organ within the military of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And given the fact that the security organ also has a crime prevention function, it would be the security organ of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I say this without trying to be humorous to my learned friend. Forget about anything you may have learned from watching American television. But in your experience, sir, in the law enforcement aspect, the internal affairs officers are the ones who are, wouldn't you agree with me, least liked by their fellow employees, because they're worried that they may or may not from time to time be investigated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you've told us about your experience, Mr. Butler. You couldn't identify in the US military whether or not there was such a department; although, you believe that there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now let's move, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He just interrupted the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Butler. Please move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the VRS, sir, can you find which organ, other than the security organ, was least liked by other people within the military, from your analysis, if you've come up with that at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, that is such an open question. Least liked by who? I mean, that is such a massively broad question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Commanders are not very well liked by sometimes their men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he needs to testify, but my question, with all due respect, says "least liked by whom," and it says "other people within." It's right there on page 72, lines 10 through 12, but we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll just ask this question: Did you ever analyse that, Mr. Butler, the relationship between, specifically, and the personal relationship between various VRS personnel and the security personnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I am aware of the fact that regardless of personalities, that by position there is going to be a natural organisational tension between the roles and responsibility of the security branch and the roles and responsibilities of other organs and the roles and responsibilities of the commander himself, I mean. So I -- I certainly took that into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now you're talking about tension here, but let's turn to another subject area, and that's the relationship between the VRS and the SDS. Do you know what the SDS is, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in 1995, you knew what it was; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew what it was in 1995 with respect to the analysis. I didn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. [B/C/S spoken] Did you analyse or did anyone that you know on the investigative team analyse the relationships, whether there was tension or if it was strained or even hostile, between the VRS and the SDS from 1992 through 1995, given that you're giving us, in some part, with all due respect, a historical analysis of what may have occurred at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did, particularly for the period of 1995, because it was relevant to my analysis. So I did, in fact, explore that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where can I find it in your pieces of work, if you will, such as the narrative, the revision, and the brigade, corps and Main Staff analysis that you've written?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you would find references to that. The specific incidence that I draw to is the 4 August 1995 firing of General Mladic as the commander of the Main Staff and moving him to be the personal adviser to President Karadzic, who assumes personal command of the military, and the next day the military generals on the Main Staff subsequently publish a letter basically saying that they're not going to recognise President Karadzic's authority to do that. I believe I encapsulate what you're talking about in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about prior to that, anything prior, leading up to July of 1995? Did you ever analyse - I haven't seen it in your report, with all due respect, but I'm sure you'll correct me if I'm wrong - the relationship between the VRS and the SDS in order to determine whether there was tension, whether it was strained, or whether it was hostile at some point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was generally aware, when I was doing my analysis, that it was. However, during the period of the construction of the reports, I did not have documentary evidence that reflected that. Clearly, and I think as part of my testimony, I mean, we have seen documentary evidence where that relationship had deteriorated to a point where, by March of 1995, the army believed that people from the SDS were actually out to assassinate key leadership figures. So while I kept that issue in mind about the strained relationship between the two, in my report, I did not have documentation which I could cite back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so I'm clear, on page 74, line 13 through 14, you, in answer to my question, state, "I was generally aware, when I was doing my analysis, that it was." And you're saying that you were aware that there was tension and a strained relationship, if not hostile relationship, between the VRS and SDS during the time frame that we're discussing; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, 1995 and particularly the middle portion of the year, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just quickly to turn to the relationship between the VRS and the MUP, which we know the acronym stands for Ministry of Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, that relationship, what -- did you analyse at all the relationship between the VRS and the MUP leading up to July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where is that located in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe - and, again, if it's not in my report, it's because the information wasn't available at the time, but I talked about it as an exhibit certainly in the Blagojevic case. I don't know if we've discussed it in this case - the fact that the relationship between the army and the MUP was acrimonious, because soldiers would frequently desert from their military units and try to sign on with MUP units in part because the MUP was paying their soldiers in cash and not other forms of either credit or script; and that particularly from an army perspective, the MUP was not returning those soldiers back to the military units, and that was having a significant impact on the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you're discussing that the relationship between the army and the MUP was acrimonious and that it had a significant impact on the VRS, isn't it true that the period of time you're discussing, sir, is the period of March, April, May, June, and July 1995, among other periods?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, through July 1995, there are references where particularly General Mladic was not a fan of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Mr. President, I ask, and I know it's 20 minutes before the break, but if I can just have the break now, I think I'm done, and I think it's within the -- within the time period that I've asked for, and I would like to take the break now so I could just go over a couple of materials. And I promise I won't be more than 15 minutes, if that, when I return. I'd like to consult with my colleague and my client, of course, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have -- unless Mr. Bourgon objects to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I'll be ready to go immediately when my colleague sits down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you of informing of that, Mr. Bourgon. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've been informed informally by both Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic that they don't think they'll be into US issues, and so, in that event, I think my colleague will be leaving, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not going to interfere or intervene in that. It's up to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SCHILDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think given the other issues I have at the office, I would take this opportunity to depart, but I will be certainly available should any issues that require my attention arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. So we'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, Mr. President. I did not object during the questioning because of the presence of Mr. Butler, but you recall when Mr. Ostojic was questioning Mr. Butler about Mr. Cerovic and whether or not the OTP had interviewed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, we did interview him in September of 2005, and that was, of course, after Mr. Butler left. I just wanted to clarify that, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring Mr. Butler in, please. At the end of the sitting, we'll be calling upon you to respond orally to the latest Prosecution motion for the addition of another witness. The Prosecution has filed a motion yesterday, I think, for the addition of another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A few more questions, Mr. Butler, just to tidy up a little bit. We were speaking of the tension or acrimonious relationship between the VRS and the MUP, and your answer, certainly with respect to General Mladic, was that he was not a fan of the MUP. My question specifically, with respect to the relationship, was that: Am I not correct, sir, that the MUP was also or had tension and strained relationships with the army, insofar as that the MUP also were not fans of the VRS. So it would work both ways; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that as a fact. I mean, I am aware of what the army's criticisms of the MUP were. I am not aware of what potential criticisms that the MUP would have had of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify a couple of other issues, if I may. You spoke of an UN person that I think has placed Mr. Beara purportedly, on or about -- on or about the area of Nova Kasaba. Are you familiar that he places allegedly Mr. Beara at Nova Kasaba at a certain time and date; and if so, do you know what time and date he places him purportedly at Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he places him there at a certain date. I don't recollect when I -- when that date is at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's a dispute between my learned friends, but it was some time, I believe, the 14th of July, 1995. Does that refresh your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be the case. I just don't remember the exact date. I mean, if it is, in fact, the 14th, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because it was in relation to my questions with respect to Srebrenica and the evacuation, and my time period was clearly up through July 12th, I just didn't want the record to be confused or unclear as to whether or not you believed that this UN person places my client anywhere near any of those areas, including Nova Kasaba, prior to the 14th of July, 1995, allegedly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the context of what we're talking about with the movement of civilians out of Potocari, that would have concluded by 2000 hours on the 13th, so you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple other issues, if I can tidy up. I'd like -- we talked about the minefields and the landmines that were present, and we discussed the number of deaths as a result of the legitimate military combat engagements. Are you familiar with a report from the United Nations, UNPROFOR, actually, protection force, dated the 17th of July, 1995, where they discuss a number of Bosnian Muslims who were killed on their way to Tuzla as a result of mines and BSA engagements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I have seen a lot of UN reports during that time frame. If you care to show me the document and refresh my memory, I can probably give you a more accurate picture, whether I recall it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can have 1D374 on the screen for Mr. Butler, please, and if I can just direct -- well, we'll show him the first page as well, in all fairness to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this is a document, sir, that we, I think, have used a couple of times in this case. It's something that was drafted by a person, Edward Joseph, as you can see in the third box on the right-hand side. It was released by an officer, Ken Biser, do you see that, with a signature accompanying his typewritten name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could look at the actual context of the document. I couldn't tell you, offhand, just looking at the header data.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please, on the text?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll return, when you let us know you've reviewed it, to the second and third pages of this document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next page, please. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for letting us know, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next, there we go. Next page, please. I cannot say that I've specifically seen this report. I don't recall. However, I do recall seeing, in other UN reports, essentially the same information, so it may have well been that it was incorporated into this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to focus, if we can quickly, on page 2 of this report, the first paragraph and the third subsection of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if you could see, sir, the UNMOs and Civil Affairs are reporting to UNPROFOR in that third subsection that, "up to 3.000 were killed on the way, mostly by mines and BSA engagements." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, contextually speaking, why that isn't included anywhere in any of your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why the document and information or why the -- or why the issue of how many were killed on the way isn't in the report? In the document, it looks like a UN Rule 70 document, which is why I wouldn't have included it. As I testified prior, the information, how many people were killed on the way with respect to combat activities, was not relevant for the analysis that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But is there -- do you have, as you sit here, sir, any doubt as to the veracity of what Mr. Biser and Mr. Joseph have reported, that up to 3.000 were killed on the way, mostly by mines and BSA engagements? Did you analyse that to see if it was accurate at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, again, because I did not detail through the combat activities and the casualty rates of the column, I have no way of knowing whether that number is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know of anyone while you were here, the investigative team, who conducted this analysis at all, whether it be your commander or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that anyone looked at specifically trying to determine the number of combat-related casualties from the column, regardless of how they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we talked about the combat engagements. Do you know where these people, who they reference as of the 17th of July, 1995, where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't know where and under what circumstances these casualties were -- were buried. My understanding of the situation was that because of the danger of mines, that at least in the initial years following the hostilities, that there was no effort to collect these individuals and bury them at all. They were left and are often referred to as surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll discuss that with other people, but let me ask you this, if I may: Not only, as you say, you don't know that anyone looked at it, isn't it a fact that no one looked at this issue at all from the investigative team during the time that you were with the Office of the Prosecution? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, my understanding is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in reading some of your testimony in Blagojevic, there was a point where you were asked about your relationship with the Office of the Prosecution, and I'm summarising just for the sake of time. At one point, it's my recollection that you said that the last two years of your engagement with the Office of the Prosecution, you were hired by them. Prior to that, you were just a liaison, loaned from the United States military. Is there -- am I recalling that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your status was always that you were a United States military employee at the service of the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My status for the first five years was that I was seconded to the OTP, loaned if you will, for the purpose of assisting in doing analysis. I was never a liaison. I was not a conduit of information going back and forth. My final two years here, I was no longer in the United States Army and I was here under a contract. So I was, I guess for lack of a better word, a UN civil servant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you were under contract, so that means from the year 2001 through 2003; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: September 2001 through September 2003, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were paid through the Office of the Prosecution, correct, for those two years?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because I wasn't sure if during the direct testimony, when you gave us the 75 per cent/25 per cent for your education that the US government paid. Prior to 2001, you were paid by the United States military; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I received a military salary. That was my compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify that. One last area that I'm going to ask you about that you touched upon, and that is the whereabouts of a General Mladic on the evening of July 14th and 15th. I think in your testimony - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that you have information that you've gleaned or reviewed that he was, in fact, in Belgrade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The body of information that's available to me reflects that he is in Belgrade starting the -- or he leaves the Main Staff and then is in Belgrade. He arrives there early evening hours of the 14th and remains there through the 15th, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we can be more precise, when does he leave the Main Staff on the 14th, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there's an intercept that we attribute General Mladic saying that somewhere around 1500 he's, "going to the field." So I take that as the time that he was anticipating leaving the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what time did he return, if at all, in the evening or late hours of the 15th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that I have clear visibility on when General Mladic would have returned from Belgrade and whether or not the Main Staff was his first destination. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where is the next time that you have visibility of General Mladic after his visit in Belgrade on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, and, again, I'd like to look back at the documents, but I believe, somewhere around either the 16th or the 17th, there may be a Main Staff document that reflects his name and says "S.R.," and I can't swear to that as a fact right now, because my memory is just not getting around that. I believe, also, that there has been, at least in the form of a statement to the OTP, one Main Staff officer has discussed the fact that he did personally see General Mladic at the Main Staff headquarters on the 17th. So, I mean, that's my broad framework of my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you analyse who was the security detail, if any, that General Mladic took with him on the 14th at approximately 1500 hours, up to and including the 16th or 17th, 1995, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you investigate who the driver was that took General Mladic, assuming, of course, that he didn't drive himself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, to be honest, I don't know that he drove. He may well have gone by helicopter. I just don't know how he got to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone on your investigative team analyse who was with Mr. Mladic or how he got there, how long he stayed, and when he returned, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the investigative team, and I believe individuals have testified, with respect to General Mladic's presence in Belgrade at various meetings on the 14th and the 15th. I don't believe that there was a component of the investigation with respect to how General Mladic got to Belgrade, and I don't believe investigatively anyone looked at how General Mladic returned from Belgrade and at what time. So I think that -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the other variable to my question? Who else may have been with him during that time period? The investigation, was there one conducted with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Bourgon starts to cross-examine Mr. Butler, I missed your words immediately after the break about the response you anticipate to the motion which was filed by the Prosecution late yesterday evening. To be honest, I would prefer it if you didn't insist upon a response to that today. We haven't, owing to the lateness of the hour of the receipt of the motion and the state of the evidence in the case and our preparation for cross-examination of this witness, had the opportunity to coordinate our response to it. It is said in the motion to particularly affect my client, and at this point in time I've neither seen the transcript of what this witness said, nor heard the CD of what he said, nor had the opportunity to consult with my client about what response I should offer. If you insist that the matter is so very urgent that we must deal with it today, then I would anticipate you are likely to receive several submissions of length from a number of Defence teams, and it may be wise to send Mr. Butler back to his hotel in about ten minutes' time. But my initial submission is that you don't deal with that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When do you think you would be in a position to come with your response? Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So we'll receive submissions tomorrow, at the end of the day. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning or good afternoon, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My name is Stefan Bourgon, and I represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. Kind of a strange place to meet after all these years, isn't it, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sure we'll be fine, and I'll try to keep my cross-examination as short as possible. The first thing I would like to look into is duties and responsibilities of the assistant commander for security, and to focus on your report or what you included in your VRS command responsibility report. You've testified about this report already; and, first, I'd like to look at the sources which you considered to be important in order to understand the functions of the assistant commander for security. So, in your report, at the end - I can't really give you a page number, because at the end it says "a" and "b" - you remember 18 different sources that you consulted to compile your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I remember that generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I'd like to go over some of these just to discuss how you looked at these sources and whether you thought they were important to understand the duties and responsibilities of the assistant commander for security. The first such reference is called "The Brigade Rules for Infantry, Motorised, Mountain, Alpine, Marine, and Light Brigades," dated 18 July 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That is 65 ter 694.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I believe that you referred to this document as being the brigade rules. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 1.7 of I'll say "your report" - and at this stage, I refer specifically to your VRS brigade command responsibility report, which was 65 ter 684 - in paragraph 1.7, you state that the primary reference defining JNA regulations on brigade-level operations and responsibilities in peacetime and in wartime is indeed those brigade rules; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't see the document, but I agree with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At any time, if you want to see one of those documents, I'll try, unless it's really necessary, not to show you the document; but if you feel there's a need, do not hesitate. Now, you would agree with me that this document includes the basis for the rules and responsibilities of the brigade commander, the brigade staff, as well as other branches of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that, of course, this was beyond any doubt an important source for you in analysing the duties of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This was an important source.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second source that I'd like to refer to is the Rules of Service of Security Organs in the Armed Forces of the SFRY, dated 21 March of 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was referred to as being 65 ter number 407, and we'll use the short title "Rules for Security Organs."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This was source 17 in your VRS brigade responsibility report. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 3.13 of your command responsibility report, you refer to this -- you refer to this manual in a number of -- on a number of issues to highlight the duties and responsibilities of the assistant commander for security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that this is also an important source to understand the duties and responsibilities of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, there's another manual I would like to show you, which is called "The Directions on the Methods and Means of Work of JNA Security Organs," which is dated 1 August 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 3D275 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I will use for this manual the title "Methods and Means of Work of Security Organs." My first question is: While this was indicated in number 19 of your sources, but it was never referred to in your brigade command responsibility report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you aware of this publication and have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree that because it is an application of the Rules for Security Organs, that it would have been an important publication to refer to in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, insomuch that, you know, I referred to it as a document that I had reviewed and referenced. However, given the technical aspects of the material involved for what I was doing the responsibility reports for, there did not appear to be much pertinent information. So, while I'm aware of this and I have reviewed it, that explains why it's not cited by footnote in my brigade reports, or the corps report, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Of course, we will have the opportunity, as part of our Defence case, to bring a different point of view. I'd just like to confirm what you've just mentioned, that the information contained in this publication was not pertinent for your analysis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not -- I didn't say it wasn't pertinent for my analysis. Because I read it, it was pertinent for my analysis. What I'm saying is that because it involved mostly technical issues related to how clandestine sources are run, how counter-intelligence plans are made, things of that nature, it wasn't relevant in respect to the broader issue of the rules and responsibilities. These are more like the "how to" manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what if I suggest to you that in this manual is the only place where you find any source or any reference to the relationship which may exist between prisoners of war and the assistant commander for security? Would that raise the level or the relevancy of this manual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm not sure that your broader statement is true, but certainly any reference to the responsibilities of the security branch and prisoners of war would be of interest, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yesterday, or the day before, you were asked a question by my colleague representing Mr. Popovic to the fact that you did not find any reference to a relationship which exists between assistant commander for security and prisoners of war. That was, of course, in the Rules on Security, and you confirmed that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that if this manual highlights that relationship, it is something that is missing from your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, if I recall correctly, the highlighted relationship between the security branch and prisoners of war in this manual has more to do with operative possibilities of taking prisoners of war and creating collection agents out of them, as opposed to the handling of them during a tactical state. That is why, in that particular context, I didn't see it as relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Later on we'll go into the prisoner of war issues in more detail, and we'll go into the specific provisions of this manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's move on to another source, which is called "The Service Regulations of the SFRY Armed Forces Military Police," 24 September 1985, 65 ter number 707.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it you're familiar with this publication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The short title we can use for this one is "Military Police Regulations," and this was source 18 in your brigade command responsibility report. Now, you agree, in paragraph 3.15 of your report --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise. I will slow down for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, in paragraph 3.15 of your brigade command responsibility report, you discuss the relationship between the officer in charge of the security body and the commander of the brigade with respect to military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, in this respect, this -- those service regulations for military police are relevant, and they were used in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to have in e-court, please, 3D276.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I'd like you to take a look at this manual, which is called "The Instruction on the Application of Regulations of the SFRY Armed Forces Military Police." We can use, as a short title, "The Instruction on Military Police Regulations." Now, to the best of my recollection, this was not included in the sources to your brigade command responsibility report, nor was it referred to or footnoted in the same report. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question, whether you were aware and whether you had seen this publication, which is only available, to the best of my knowledge, in the B/C/S language. If I tell you, Mr. Butler, that this publication deals specifically with the interaction between military police and prisoners of war, would you agree that this was indeed a source that maybe should have been consulted in drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under that hypothetical, if I had had access to it, it might very well have, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
