utterances.text: Is that something -- a publication that you looked for, considering the fact that it is the application of the military police rules? Is that -- did you expect or look for such a publication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As part of the investigative process and part of the analytical process that I was undertaking, we actively looked for all such regulations that would relate with respect to command and with respect to security, so that we could identify them and get them translated to determine, you know, where they fit into the broader picture. So that was an effort that we did undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But this one, you yourself never found?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I take it -- I take it from the ERN range of 046 that this is a document that would have hit the OTP long after my departure. It has a very late ERN number on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, then, that to a certain extent, not having consulted this manual, that your brigade command responsibility report is incomplete?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In light of the fact that there may be additional information out there, I hold open the prospect that it may very well now be incomplete, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's move on to another source, which is the Instruction on Command and Control over the Security and Intelligence Organs of the VRS, which is not a publication, but rather instructions, dated 11 November 1984 and signed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 2741.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it you know what document I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by that date, sir. Are you correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, let's put it on the screen. This is 65 ter 2741, if I may have that on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will be referring to this instruction at length during my cross-examination, and I'll be referring to it as being the Main Staff Instruction on Security and Intelligence Organs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that explains it. The date is 24 October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the date would be -- maybe I misled you with the date. It is being brought to my attention now that the date is, of course, 11 November 1994, 1-9-9-4, which is the probably what the problem was why you could not recognise the instruction itself. But you know which instruction I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it up on my screen, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would agree with me that this -- this is an important document to understand the role of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 11 November 1994 is the stamp, but the directive is 24 October. Another mistake. I apologise. 24 October 1994. The other date, 11 November, is a reception stamp, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. So this, you would agree with me, is an important document to understand the role of the assistant commander for security, if only because it was drafted months before the events in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your examination-in-chief, you were referred to this publication or to this publication or to those instructions, but they were not included in the sources to your brigade command responsibility report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And they were not footnoted or referred to in the brigade command responsibility report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As I'm sure you're aware from the Blagojevic testimony, at the time that those reports were drafted, the Office of the Prosecutor had this document but was not able to get it out of a particular collection. I only became aware that we had this document and had it translated, and I did discuss it during the testimony phase of that trial. I believe this was a document that Mr. Karnavas' people found.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed. This was a document which you testified about at the Blagojevic trial. But to the extent that it was not used in your brigade command responsibility report, would you agree with me that this is another, I would say, missing part of your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the obvious conclusion is I can't include material that I do not know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that affects, of course, the validity of your report as we sit here today; would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The absence of information would potentially impact some of my conclusions, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next source I would like to refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm being told to slow down. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next source I would like to refer you to is the Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces manual under 65 ter number 710. Are you aware of this -- which manual I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I am generally. It's not up on the screen, but yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's put it up on the screen in e-court, please, 65 ter number 710. The short title of this document, I think we can use "Intelligence Support Manual."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the manual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, it was, in fact, referred to in paragraph 3.8 -- 3.18, sorry, of the VRS brigade command responsibility report; however, you did not discuss this publication during your examination-in-chief. So my question is the following, even though it was not brought up earlier: It is, indeed, an important publication if only to understand the distinction between the intelligence and the counter-intelligence functions; would you agree with me on this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now that we have these seven sources, and whether they were included or not in your report, I'd like you to simply confirm what was in your report concerning the application of the JNA doctrine to VRS in the field of security. Now, all of these sources that we've referred, other than for the Main Staff instruction of October 1994, they were all drafted and adopted years before the events of July 1995, at a time when JNA doctrine and rules were to be applied, of course, by units and members of the JNA; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me that when these regulations refer, at least today, to concepts such as the League of Communists or other similar concepts, these were not -- no longer being -- or concepts that were in use in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, nonetheless, in your report, you say, for the purposes of the VRS, and more specifically I can say the Drina Corps and its subordinate units, you maintain in your report that for the conduct of their daily activities in 1995, these regulations and doctrine did find application. Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You also stated one of the reasons for this was probably military effectiveness. The professional officers were trained using this doctrine and regulations; and, therefore, it would be normal for them to continue using it in 1995. Is that a summary of your conclusions in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, many of the officers that we have talked to over the years have confirmed that, so, you know, that's my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And another reason could be lack of time and opportunity to develop new doctrine by July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, as I expect you well appreciate, rewriting a military doctrine on the fly is not something that most states do. It requires a long educational process within the officer and leadership core of a military, so it's unsurprising that they wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that your opinion in this regard is also based on your analysis of all the documents at your disposal in order to conclude that the JNA doctrine and regulations did apply in 19 -- or was applied in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To the extent that we could when analysing through the broader body of documents, we did look for material either where it would directly relate to that or bodies of documents or orders which would either tend to confirm or deny that procedures in these JNA documents were continuing to be followed. So that was a constant process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And does your conclusion apply to the responsibilities of the brigade assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, with respect to the brigade assistant commanders for security, with the addition of the 1994 -- the October 1994 document - and I believe I testified to this fact - I believe that document tends to reinforce the fact that the brigade rules were being applied and that the security rules were being applied as envisioned by the former JNA. I don't take that document to be something different than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your conclusion, I take it, also applies to the command relationship between the military police company and the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, in your view, on the basis of the analysis of all the material at your disposal, would I be right in saying that it is not possible that those issues - I'm talking about the brigade commander to military police command relationship and security organ issues - that they were governed any differently in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I agree. I have not found any substantial or any body of evidence that would suggest that there was some form of another command structure in place. The -- the leadership and command structure, as it was envisioned in the brigade and security rules back in the 1980s, appeared to be in place in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you stated, this Main Staff instruction on security and intelligence of October 1995 did not modify and was in accordance with the application of the JNA doctrine and regulations? The matter of security, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, there may have been some technical issues addressed, but I -- by and large, they did not alter the regulatory relationships and they did not alter the command relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a little earlier that you spoke to a number of people on this issue, that you conducted some interviews. Were you informed by the Office of the Prosecution that some witnesses in this case may have offered different conclusions on the issues of security or on the issue of the command relationship between commander of the brigade and military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would that change your conclusions, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He would require to know the details. I mean, how can you put the questions so vague and expect him to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just want to get a confirmation from you as to how firm you are concerning your conclusion of what we just discussed concerning the application of JNA doctrine and regulations in those two fields, namely, security organs affairs and command relationship between the brigade commander and the military police, and whether -- how firm you are on those conclusions in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is another hugely broad question that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, Mr. Bourgon. Let's move on, and then it can become an argument later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to another topic, Mr. Butler, before we leave each other today. I'd like simply to use your expertise to highlight the difference between security and intelligence organs. First, I take it you will agree with me that, pursuant to these regulations and doctrine we've referred to, that there are significant differences between intelligence and security functions.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For example, the intelligence officer is a member of the brigade Command Staff, and his immediate superior is the brigade Chief of Staff; while on the other hand, the security officer holds the position of assistant commander for security, and his immediate superior is the brigade commander. So that's one of the differences; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's specified in the regulations, and I believe within the context of the documents, it was applied as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, of course, if the commander is away and the Chief of Staff exercises command and control over the brigade units, in whatever capacity - I don't want to get into this debate - then the immediate superior of the assistant commander for security becomes the Chief of Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to command responsibility, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And another difference between the intelligence officer and the assistant commander for security is, indeed, the nature of the work they perform? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we look at the essence of the work performed by the intelligence officer, I suggest to you that the essence of his work is the gathering of intelligence, while the main component of the work performed by the assistant commander for security is counter-intelligence. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's a fair reading of the rules and certainly the intent behind what the VRS was trying to do at that time, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And looking specifically at the intelligence function, I take it that you, in your capacity as an intelligence warrant officer within the United States Army for many years, you are aware of the importance of intelligence gathering for the successful conduct of combat operations or combat activities within a brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence gathering as well as the successful analysis of that information, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 3.17 of your brigade command responsibility report, you describe the responsibilities of the intelligence organ, and you use, for this basis, the brigade rules. I'd like to go over quickly some of these responsibilities. So, for example, the intelligence organ will be responsible for and organises intelligence support for combat actions. Is that one of the things that the intelligence organ does?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the intelligence organ would continuously monitor and assess the enemy, and report on the enemy's condition to everyone concerned in the Command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the primary customer for the intelligence officer and his information would be the remainder of the operations staff and the commander, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it also controls the reconnaissance activities of all organs and units in the brigade; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I just refer you now to the brigade rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we can have on the e-court 694, I'd like to have -- this is the brigade rules, and I'd like to have English page 61 and B/C/S page 99.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would simply read something, to see if you agree, that the purpose of intelligence support of combat operations conducted by brigades would be to gather, process, and use intelligence about the enemy, the area of combat operations, and weather conditions in the zone of intelligence responsibility. That's what we find at paragraph 208. Does that summarise the intelligence function with respect to combat activities? It's a bit small to read. Most of the other documents I have--

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm doing fine, that's all right sir. Well, I was doing fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, again, this is paragraph 208, and I take it you must have read by now the -- at the end of this paragraph, where it says that, "in wartime, the focus is on gathering data relevant for making decisions for the deployment of forces." Is there anything in this paragraph 208 that you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As written, I think paragraph 208 is a fair reflection of the issues related to intelligence, particularly in a -- in a battlefield environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And making reference to your answer just a little earlier, you will agree with me that intelligence is very much, to use our language, talking about military language, an "ops matter." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 209, we see that the intelligence organ actually carries out intelligence support tasks, and we also see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, could you take a look? Is the text what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 209, yes, it is, but I need to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take a look at 208, whether it's the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out, because I was looking from afar and I don't think it's the right paragraph. I was looking for the brigade rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we continue this tomorrow, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed. I will just make sure I have the right references and give the right paragraph to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was fine in 208. As I read 208, it was a fair application of the battlefield. But when you started to get to 209, we talk about terrain factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that for today. Tomorrow, we will be sitting in the afternoon, you know that, not in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Of course, what I just did, I did it on purpose for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
